public_rationale: Both companies' compute commitments far exceed what their revenue and cash could cover. OpenAI projects $278 billion of negative free cash flow from 2026 to 2030 and is on track to use up its raised cash by 2028. Anthropic has about $518 billion in mostly non-cancellable commitments against about $20 billion in cash at the end of 2025. On a strict 'self-funded' reading, that leans toward the claim. But both companies have kept raising large sums and paying their bills, and Anthropic reported positive adjusted operating income for two quarters. Whether they truly 'cannot afford' the compute depends on whether future financing and revenue arrive, and on a reading of 'afford' the speaker did not supply. The evidence does not settle it.
limitations: Most figures come from press reports of private or confidential documents.
The verdict turns on what 'afford' means.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Neither OpenAI nor Anthropic can actually afford the compute they are contracting for.

statement.excerpt: Neither of these companies can actually afford this compute, but that doesn’t matter, because this data center won’t actually exist for years, if it ever does.

from_speaker: this data center won't actually exist for years, if it ever does
our_interpretation: 'This compute' refers to the Lambda/Hut 8 data-center capacity for Anthropic and, more broadly, to the large compute deals Anthropic and OpenAI have signed.
The plain reading of 'can't afford' is that, around the post date, neither company could cover these commitments from its own revenue and cash without continued outside financing.
A stricter reading is that they will be unable to pay. That is a future question and is not tested here.
The period is the state of affairs around the post date (August–September 2026). This is the evaluator's choice, because the sentence gives no period.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence from around September 2026 shows each company's committed compute spending far exceeds its revenue plus cash on hand, so that it depends on new financing to pay, and the claim's own sense of 'afford' is accepted.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence shows either company could pay its compute commitments from its own cash flow and cash on hand, without needing new outside financing.

evidence.excerpt: The FT said the company ⁠raised $122 billion in March at an $852 billion valuation but is on track ​to exhaust that cash by 2028.
evidence.explanation: OpenAI expects $278B of negative free cash flow from 2026 to 2030 and expects to run out of its raised cash by 2028. It cannot fund its compute from operations, but it is currently funded by investors.

evidence.excerpt: about 80% of the $518 billion it's committed must be paid regardless of how much computing power the company actually uses.
evidence.explanation: Anthropic's mostly non-cancellable $518B of compute commitments compare with $20.28B in cash at the end of 2025, as the same article reports. So the commitments depend on future revenue and financing.

evidence.excerpt: They are multi-year obligations against revenue that has been growing quickly but has not yet reached the scale the contracts assume.
evidence.explanation: This supports the view that current revenue does not cover the contracts. The same article calls the arithmetic 'defensible' given that Anthropic's run rate had passed $30bn.

evidence.excerpt: Anthropic has told ⁠shareholders that its adjusted ‌operating income will be positive for a second ​straight quarter
evidence.explanation: Anthropic was operating profitably on an adjusted basis, which weakens a flat claim that it cannot afford compute. It does not show it can cover hundreds of billions in commitments.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A missed, cancelled or forcibly renegotiated compute payment by either company would settle it against them. Sustained self-funded payment of their commitments would settle it the other way.
